method_note: FAST MODE, one round. Reused facts copied from earlier packs with their sources (reused: true). New facts read today from official sources only.

facts.claim: Italy (US Embassy guidance): a civil ceremony is performed by the mayor or a deputy. Two witnesses (any nationality, over 18, valid photo ID) and, if needed, an interpreter must be present; a witness cannot serve as interpreter.
facts.publisher: US Embassy and Consulates in Italy
facts.use_note: Written for US citizens, but the ceremony itself is the same Italian civil ceremony for Australians (the comune runs it under the Italian Civil Code). Medium because the source is a US page; Italian official confirmation sought below. The comune (Ufficio di Stato Civile) confirms the current process.

facts.claim: Italy: the US Embassy page does not bar relatives from being ceremony witnesses, while it does bar family members, future family members and in-laws from being Atto Notorio witnesses.
facts.publisher: US Embassy and Consulates in Italy
facts.use_note: Absence of a ban is not an explicit permission. Write 'relatives can usually witness the ceremony itself; confirm with the comune'. The comune confirms the current process.

facts.claim: Italy, Australian route: Australians marrying in Italy need a Nulla Osta from the Australian Embassy in Rome. To get it, they first obtain an Atto Notorio, signed by the Australian citizen and four witnesses not related to the couple, either at the Italian consulate for their state of residence in Australia or at any tribunal in Italy. The Atto Notorio is valid 6 months.
facts.publisher: Consulate of Italy in Adelaide (Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs)
facts.use_note: These are paperwork witnesses, not ceremony witnesses. Keep the two apart in the article. The Italian consulate for the couple's state confirms the current process.

facts.claim: Italy, US route only (for contrast): Italian consulates in New York and Los Angeles ask for four Atto Notorio witnesses over 18 and unrelated; San Francisco says two witnesses per spouse; the US Embassy page says two.
facts.publisher: Consolato Generale d'Italia a New York
facts.use_note: DO NOT USE for Australians. Recorded to show it was checked. Australians follow F-102.

facts.claim: Greece (Heraklion): each person marrying must be accompanied by an adult witness. The witness may be a relative, even a first-degree one, and must bring an identity card or, for foreigners, a passport.
facts.use_note: Two witnesses in total. Other municipalities may differ. The municipality's civil registry (Lixiarchio) confirms the current process.

facts.claim: Fiji: foreigners marrying in Fiji need passports, a Certificate of Single Status, Certificate of Search or Certificate of No Legal Impediment, divorce or death papers if relevant, and two witnesses with photo ID.
facts.use_note: No minimum age stated on this page. The Registrar General's Office (Fiji BDM) confirms the current process.

facts.claim: France: a marriage must take place at a town hall (mairie) to be legally recognised, and at least one of the applicants must be a French citizen or a legal resident of France.
facts.use_note: Witness rules matter only if one partner qualifies. The mairie confirms the current process.

facts.claim: Indonesia (including Bali): for non-Muslim marriages, couples lodge a Notice of Intention to Marry with the Civil Registry Office at least 10 days before the wedding and the marriage must be registered there to be legal. Both parties must hold the same religion recognised by the Indonesian Government.
facts.use_note: Context for witness facts. The Civil Registry Office (Dinas Kependudukan dan Pencatatan Sipil) confirms the current process.
